paragraphs.text: This is what is wont to happen to those who break up the one doctrine of the faith into the divergent meanings of sects, and search out only those testimonies from the divine Scriptures by which they may establish their own doctrine, while as for the resolutions of those statements of divine Scripture which come from the opposite side, they do not touch them even with the tip of the finger, as the Lord says. But he who faithfully and soundly gathers the meaning of the sacred Volumes ought to show how those things which seem to be contrary are not truly contrary.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: We shall therefore attempt, in the present passage also, to show how this that follows does not conflict with our earlier exposition. We have often said, and said more plainly in the preface, that the Apostle in this Epistle makes mention of many laws in such a way that, when he passes from one to another, it can scarcely be detected except by a sufficiently attentive reader.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: He had said in the foregoing, that “through the law is the knowledge of sin”; and because he perceived that it could be answered: Therefore if from the natural law there is knowledge of sin, there can be from it also knowledge of righteousness — namely according to that image of the art of medicine which we gave above: that just as through it sickness is known so that health may be found, so also, if through the law of nature knowledge of sin can come about, in like manner knowledge of righteousness can also come about.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: Since, then, he had seen that this could be objected to him, after he said, “For through the law is the knowledge of sin,” he adds: “But now, apart from the law, the righteousness of God has been manifested.” Such, then, is what he says: Not as the knowledge of sin comes through the law, so also does the manifestation of God's righteousness come through the law; but apart from the law the righteousness of God is manifested. For the law of nature could convict the nature of sin, and display knowledge of it; but the righteousness of God transcends and towers above anything whatsoever that the human mind can probe by natural perceptions alone.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: For it does not suffice for understanding and considering not just any human righteousness, but the very righteousness of God, and the judgments which descend from it, of which it is said that they are “a great deep,” and that so profound is the righteousness of God and his judgments that the Apostle says: “How unsearchable are the judgments of God!” But Wisdom too speaks to men as though the righteousness of God cannot be known by the motions of nature alone, but must be sought through the pursuit of teaching; and therefore it says: “Learn righteousness, you who judge the earth.” Wherefore for coming to know the righteousness of God the law of nature will help not at all, even though it seems to perceive something about human righteousness.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: For that law can perceive what is just among men, namely that what a man does not wish to suffer himself, this he should not do to his neighbor. Can it naturally perceive anything of that righteousness which says: “See that you do not do your righteousness before men”; and, “that your left hand may not know what your right hand does”? These and such things the law of nature cannot call just; and therefore the Apostle says: “But now, apart from the law” — that is, of nature — “the righteousness of God has been manifested,” having the testimony of the law of Moses and of the prophets, in which the Holy Spirit had written many things about the righteousness of God through figures and riddles.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: And I would not have you wonder that one word “law,” placed twice in the same passage, signifies different things. We find this to be the custom of Scripture in other places as well: as there: “Do you not say that there are yet four months until the harvest comes? Lift up your eyes, and see the regions, for they are white unto harvest.” Is not in this place too the harvest, named twice, referred first to the bodily harvest, and second to the spiritual?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: And again in the Gospel, when the Savior says to the Samaritan woman, “Give me to drink,” and after her reply says again to her: “If you knew who it is that says to you: Give me to drink; you surely would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.” And again he added to her: “Everyone who drinks of this water shall thirst again; but whoever drinks of the water that I give him shall not thirst forever.” Do you see how both “to drink” and “water” are taken now indeed bodily, now spiritually, in one and the same passage? There is a similar instance placed there, where the man blind from birth is healed.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: After this the Savior says: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.” Is not here too both seeing and not seeing understood now bodily, now spiritually? So therefore also in this place, when the Apostle says that the righteousness of God is manifested apart from the law, the law of nature is understood; but when he says: “Being witnessed to by the law and the prophets,” he designates the law of Moses.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: But if what we have said still seems to you insufficiently clear, we shall add these considerations as well: If it appears that the law of which it is said, "But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law," is the same as that of which he says, "attested by the law and the prophets" — then, if indeed it has been manifested apart from the law, it does not receive the testimony of the law; but if it receives testimony from the law, then it has not been manifested apart from the law. Since this difficulty is insoluble and cannot by any reasoning be broken down, it must be said that the righteousness of God is indeed manifested through Christ Jesus, with testimony borne to him not by the law of nature, which is still in every way slight and small, but by the law of Moses — not that law which is according to the letter, but that which is according to the spirit, concerning which the same Apostle says, "For the law is spiritual." And likewise the prophets bear witness through the Spirit of God who spoke in them. There is besides, in the Apostle's usage regarding this expression, a remarkable distinction, if anyone observes it more carefully.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: It is the custom among the Greeks to place before nouns what they call ἄρθρα (arthra), which among us may be termed "articles." Whenever, therefore, he names the law of Moses, he prefixes to the noun the customary article; but whenever he wishes the natural law to be understood, he names the law without the article. And so in this place too, where he says, "Now apart from law the righteousness of God has been manifested," it has no article; but in what follows, where he says, "attested by the law and the prophets," in this second place he has set "law" with the article.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: If, then, the difference in the use of the term "law" has been sufficiently made plain, let us now see what righteousness is manifested apart from the natural law. The same apostle Paul says of Christ that he "has been made for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption." This righteousness of God, therefore, which is Christ, is manifested apart from the natural law indeed, yet not apart from the law of Moses or the prophets.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: For the law gives testimony to him, just as he himself says: "Search the Scriptures; they are the ones that bear witness concerning me." For the natural law can indeed furnish occasions and give understanding, as we have said, either toward those things which equity demands be done among men, or toward this very thing, that one should perceive that God exists. But who can perceive by nature concerning Christ that he is the Son of God? Therefore it is apart from this law that the righteousness of God, which is Christ, has been manifested, attested by the law of Moses and the prophets.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: But before we hasten on to what follows, it does not seem that even this observation should be passed over: that in the case of sin he set down "recognition," but in the case of righteousness "manifestation." For "everything that is manifested is light"; and if what is manifested is light, then sin, which is not light, is not manifested but recognized. I understand in this way also that saying: "There is nothing hidden that shall not be manifested, nor covered that shall not be revealed." But let us return to our subject.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: The righteousness which has been given to us freely by God, not acquired by our effort, has been made plain without the written law, and having been hidden in the law has been revealed with greater clarity by the examples of Christ, which are more obvious. The law and the prophets foretold that this righteousness would come in the last times, or perhaps this means that they both bore witness to the recognition of sin.
paragraphs.author: Pelagius
paragraphs.work: PELAGIUS'S COMMENTARY ON ROMANS

paragraphs.text: It was once the law; now it is "the righteousness of God which is by the faith of (Jesus) Christ." What means this distinction? Has your god been subserving the interests of the Creator's dispensation, by affording time to Him and to His law? Is the "Now" in the hands of Him to whom belonged the "Then"? Surely, then, the law was His, whose is now the righteousness of God.
paragraphs.author: Tertullian
paragraphs.work: Against Marcion Book V

paragraphs.text: What else comes through faith in Jesus Christ except the righteousness of God which is the revelation of Christ? For it is by faith in the revelation of Jesus Christ that the gift long ago promised by God is acknowledged and received.
paragraphs.author: Ambrosiaster
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON PAUL'S EPISTLES

paragraphs.text: How could Paul have promised glory, honor and peace to the good works of Gentiles apart from the grace of the gospel? Because there otherwise is no acceptance of persons with God. And because it is not the hearers but the doers of the law who are justified, he argues that all, whether Jew or Gentile, shall alike have salvation in the gospel.
paragraphs.author: Augustine of Hippo
paragraphs.work: THE SPIRIT AND THE LETTER 44

paragraphs.text: Paul says "for all" meaning first the Jews, in that it was from among them that salvation first arose, and then the Gentiles, in that from the Jews grace had abounded even to them so that now both share in it together. This grace is not given in general but only to those "who believe," but it is common to all these without distinction.
paragraphs.author: Gennadius of Constantinople
paragraphs.work: PAULINE COMMENTARY FROM THE GREEK CHURCH

paragraphs.text: After saying, "the righteousness of God," he adds straightway, "by faith unto all and upon all that believe." Here again the Jew is alarmed by his not having anything better than the rest, and being numbered with the whole world. Now that he may not feel this, he again lowers him with fear by adding, "For there is no difference, for all have sinned." For tell me not that it is such and such a Greek, such and such a Scythian, such and such a Thracian, for all are in the same plight.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on Romans 7

paragraphs.text: For even if you have received the Law, one thing alone is there which you have learnt from the Law-to know sin, not to flee from it. Next, that they may say, "even if we have sinned, still it is not in the same way that they did," he added, "and have come short of the glory of God." So that even if you have not done the same sins as others, still you are alike bereft of the glory, since you belong to those who have offended, and he that hath offended belongeth not to such as are glorified, but to such as are put to shame. Yet, be not afraid: for the reason of my saying this was not that I might thrust you into despair, but that I might show the love of the Lord toward man.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on Romans 7

paragraphs.text: The law, then, and the prophets are witnesses of the righteousness of God; and this righteousness is manifested through faith in Jesus Christ unto all who believe, among whom there is no distinction, whether they believe from among the Jews or from among the Gentiles. But observe that for the manifesting of God's righteousness he laid down not one cause only, that of faith, but joined to it also the law and the prophets — because neither does faith alone, without the law and the prophets, manifest the righteousness of God, nor again do the law and the prophets without faith: the one therefore cleaves to the other, so that from both there may be perfection.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: This refers to the faith by which one believes in Jesus Christ. In this there is no distinction between Jew and Gentile.
paragraphs.author: Pelagius
paragraphs.work: PELAGIUS'S COMMENTARY ON ROMANS

paragraphs.text: This includes both Jews and Greeks. For all here includes even the saints in order to show that nobody can keep the law without faith. For the law was given in such a way that faith was also embedded in it. This faith looked toward a future salvation. Thus the death of Christ benefits everyone, because it has here in this world taught what is to be believed and observed, and in the future it will deliver everyone from hell.
paragraphs.author: Ambrosiaster
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON PAUL'S EPISTLES

paragraphs.text: For the apostle says: "All have sinned, and come short of the glory of God; being justified freely by His grace, through the redemption that is in Jesus Christ: whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in His blood, to declare His righteousness for the remission of sins that are past, through the forbearance of God; to declare, `I say, 'at this time His righteousness, that He might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus."
paragraphs.author: Callistus I of Rome

paragraphs.text: That it is impossible to attain to God the Father, except by His Son Jesus Christ.
paragraphs.author: Cyprian
paragraphs.work: Treatise XII Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews

paragraphs.text: In the Gospel: "I am the way, and the truth, and the life: no one cometh to the Father but by me." Also in the same place: "I am the door: by me if any man shall enter in, he shall be saved." Also in the same place: "Many prophets and righteous men have desired to see the things which ye see, and have not seen them; and to hear those things which ye hear, and have not heard them." Also in the same place: "He that believeth on the Son hath eternal life: he that is not obedient in word to the Son hath not life; but the wrath of God shall abide upon him." Also Paul to the Ephesians: "And when He had come, He preached peace to you, to those which are afar off, and peace to those which are near, because through Him we both have access in one Spirit unto the Father." Also to the Romans: "For all have sinned, and fail of the glory of God; but they are justified by His gift and grace, through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus." Also in the Epistle of Peter the apostle: "Christ hath died once for our sins, the just for the unjust, that He might present us to God." Also in the same place: "For in this also was it preached to them that are dead, that they might be raised again." Also in the Epistle of John: "Whosoever denieth the Son, the same also hath not the Father. He that confesseth the Son, hath both the Son and the Father."
paragraphs.author: Cyprian
paragraphs.work: Treatise XII Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews

paragraphs.text: It was for this reason, too, that the Lord descended into the regions beneath the earth, preaching His advent there also, and [declaring] the remission of sins received by those who believe in Him. Now all those believed in Him who had hope towards Him, that is, those who proclaimed His advent, and submitted to His dispensations, the righteous men, the prophets, and the patriarchs, to whom He remitted sins in the same way as He did to us, which sins we should not lay to their charge, if we would not despise the grace of God. For as these men did not impute unto us (the Gentiles) our transgressions, which we wrought before Christ was manifested among us, so also it is not right that we should lay blame upon those who sinned before Christ's coming.
paragraphs.author: Irenaeus
paragraphs.work: Against Heresies Book IV

paragraphs.text: For "all men come short of the glory of God," and are not justified of themselves, but by the advent of the Lord,-they who earnestly direct their eyes towards His light. And it is for our instruction that their actions have been committed to writing, that we might know, in the first place, that our God and theirs is one, and that sins do not please Him although committed by men of renown; and in the second place, that we should keep from wickedness.
paragraphs.author: Irenaeus
paragraphs.work: Against Heresies Book IV

paragraphs.text: For if these men of old time, who preceded us in the gifts [bestowed upon them], and for whom the Son of God had not yet suffered, when they committed any sin and served fleshly lusts, were rendered objects of such disgrace, what shall the men of the present day suffer, who have despised the Lord's coming, and become the slaves of their own lusts?
paragraphs.author: Irenaeus
paragraphs.work: Against Heresies Book IV

paragraphs.text: And truly the death of the Lord became [the means of] healing and remission of sins to the former, but Christ shall not die again in behalf of those who now commit sin, for death shall no more have dominion over Him; but the Son shall come in the glory of the Father, requiring from His stewards and dispensers the money which He had entrusted to them, with usury; and from those to whom He had given most shall He demand most. We ought not, therefore, as that presbyter remarks, to be puffed up, nor be severe upon those of old time, but ought ourselves to fear, lest perchance, after [we have come to] the knowledge of Christ, if we do things displeasing to God, we obtain no further forgiveness of sins, but be shut out from His kingdom. And therefore it was that Paul said, "For if [God] spared not the natural branches, [take heed] lest He also spare not thee, who, when thou wert a wild olive tree, wert grafted into the fatness of the olive tree, and wert made a partaker of its fatness."
paragraphs.author: Irenaeus
paragraphs.work: Against Heresies Book IV

paragraphs.text: We ought not, therefore, as that presbyter remarks, to be puffed up, nor be severe upon those of old time, but ought ourselves to fear, lest perchance, after [we have come to] the knowledge of Christ, if we do things displeasing to God, we obtain no further forgiveness of sins, but be shut out from His kingdom.
paragraphs.author: Irenaeus
paragraphs.work: Against Heresies Book IV

paragraphs.text: There is, he says, no distinction between Jews and Greeks, since it is established that all alike have been made subject to sin, as was shown above, and that now the righteousness of God, supported by the testimonies of the law and the prophets, has been given through faith in Jesus Christ alike to all. From the fact that all had been made subject to sin, they were without doubt made strangers also to the glory of God, since they could neither receive it in any way nor merit it. For how would a sinner dare to give glory to God, to whom the Prophet says: "But to the sinner God said: Why do you declare my righteous decrees?" And again another Scripture says: "Praise of God is not comely in the mouth of a sinner."
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: All sinners need the glory of God because they do not have their own.
paragraphs.author: Pelagius
paragraphs.work: PELAGIUS'S COMMENTARY ON ROMANS

paragraphs.text: Paul shows that nature has failed the Gentiles and that both nature and the law have failed the Jews, before going on to mention the grace of the gospel and saying: "What do we have by grace which is special and superior? Faith, made effective by the righteousness of Christ." … Paul does not say that all have broken the law but that all have sinned in a general sense. Now the one who is lacking something tries to make up his deficiency. The Jews had the law, but they were lacking the fullness of grace.
paragraphs.author: Severian of Gabala
paragraphs.work: PAULINE COMMENTARY FROM THE GREEK CHURCH

paragraphs.text: They are justified freely because they have not done anything nor given anything in return, but by faith alone they have been made holy by the gift of God. Paul testifies that the grace of God is in Christ, because we have been redeemed by Christ according to the will of God so that once set free we may be justified, as he says to the Galatians: "Christ redeemed us by offering himself for us." For he achieved this despite the fierce attacks of the devil, who was outwitted. For the devil received Christ (in hell) thinking that he could hold him there, but because he could not withstand his power he lost not only Christ but all those whom he held at the same time.
paragraphs.author: Ambrosiaster
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON PAUL'S EPISTLES

paragraphs.text: "Being justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus: Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in His blood, to declare His righteousness." See by how many proofs he makes good what was said. First, from the worthiness of the person, for it is not a man who doeth these things, that He should be too weak for it, but God all-powerful. For it is to God, he says, that the righteousness belongs. Again, from the Law and the Prophets. For you need not be afraid at hearing the "without the Law," inasmuch as the Law itself approves this. Thirdly, from the sacrifices under the old dispensation.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on Romans 7

paragraphs.text: For it was on this ground that he said, "In His blood," to call to their minds those sheep and calves. For if the sacrifices of things without reason, he means, cleared from sin, much more would this blood. And he does not say barely "redemption," but "entire redemption," to show that we should come no more into such slavery.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on Romans 7

paragraphs.text: And for this same reason he calls it a propitiation, to show that if the type had such force, much more would the reality display the same. But to show again that it was no novel thing or recent, he says, "fore-ordained;" and by saying God "fore-ordained," and showing that the good deed is the Father's, he showeth it to be the Son's also. For the Father "fore-ordained," but Christ in His own blood wrought the whole aright.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on Romans 7

paragraphs.text: Therefore the righteousness of God, coming through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe, whether they be Jews or Greeks, justifies them once cleansed of their former crimes, and makes them capable of the glory of God: and this he does not from their merits, nor for their works, but freely bestows glory upon those who believe. "Through the redemption," he says, "which is in Christ Jesus." Let us consider more attentively what is meant by the redemption which is in Christ Jesus. "Redemption" is the name given to what is handed over to enemies on behalf of those whom they hold in captivity, so that they may restore them to their former liberty.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: The captive multitude of the human race, then, was being held among enemies, overcome by sin as though by war: the Son of God came, who "was made for us" not only "wisdom from God, and righteousness, and sanctification," but "redemption" as well: and he gave himself as the redemption, that is, he handed himself over to the enemies, and poured out his blood for them as they thirsted for it: and this has become the redemption of believers, just as Peter also writes in his Epistle, saying: "For you were not redeemed with corruptible silver or gold, but with the precious blood of the only-begotten Son of God." Perhaps Solomon too was indicating this under a mystery when he said: "The redemption of a man's soul is his own riches." For if you inquire what the riches of the soul are, you will find that its riches are properly wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: But all these things the Apostle says are Christ. Christ, then, is the riches of the soul, and therefore he himself is its redemption. For bodily riches are to be believed rather the ruin of the soul than its redemption, unless they be turned to the good work of righteousness and mercy, and be transferred from bodily riches into riches of the soul.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: We have been justified without the works of the law, through baptism. In this way God has freely forgiven our sins even though we are undeserving. Christ has redeemed us with the blood of his death.… For we were all condemned to death, to which Christ handed himself over, though he had no need to, in order to redeem us by his blood.… Note also that Christ did not merely buy us but bought us "back," because we were once his by nature, even though we were separated from him by our sins. If we stop sinning, our redemption will indeed be profitable for us.
paragraphs.author: Pelagius
paragraphs.work: PELAGIUS'S COMMENTARY ON ROMANS

paragraphs.text: Grace is the glory of God, not the merit of him who has been freed.
paragraphs.author: Prosper of Aquitaine
paragraphs.work: GRACE AND FREE WILL 10.2

paragraphs.text: Paul says this, because in Christ God put forward, i.e., appointed, himself as a future expiation for the human race if they believed. This expiation was by his blood. We have been set free by his death so that God might reveal him and condemn death by his passion. This was in order to make his promise clear, by which he set us free from sin as he had promised before.
paragraphs.author: Ambrosiaster
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON PAUL'S EPISTLES

paragraphs.text:
And when he fulfilled this promise he showed himself to be righteous.God knew the purpose of his lovingkindness, by which he determined to come to the rescue of sinners, both those living on earth and those who were held bound in hell. He waited a very long time for both. He nullified the sentence by which it seemed just that everyone should be condemned in order to show us that long ago he had decided to liberate the human race, as he promised through Jeremiah the prophet, saying: "I will forgive their iniquity and I will remember their sin no more." And in case it might be thought that this promise was for the Jews only, he said through Isaiah: "My house will be called a house of prayer for all peoples."26
For although the promise was made to the Jews, God knew in advance that the ungodly Jews would reject his gift. Therefore he promised that he would allow the Gentiles to share in his grace.
paragraphs.author: Ambrosiaster
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON PAUL'S EPISTLES

paragraphs.text: In view of this the ungodly negligence of the Jews was thwarted.
paragraphs.author: Ambrosiaster
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON PAUL'S EPISTLES

paragraphs.text: In the inner place was set the Ark of the Propitiation, which was concealed behind the veil, and was not seen by any one. The Propitiatory was a type of the Lord Christ according to the flesh, as saith the Apostle: Whom God set forth to be a propitiation by his blood; and again the high priest was himself a type of the Lord Christ, according to the Apostle: For, saith he, just as the high priest once a year entereth into the inner Tabernacle, so Christ, having come a high priest of the good things to come through his own blood, entered in once for all into the Holy place, having obtained eternal redemption, as methinks I have frequently mentioned.
paragraphs.author: Cosmas Indicopleustes
paragraphs.work: The Christian Topography, Book 5

paragraphs.text: Christ, being an "expiation by his blood," teaches each one thinking of this to become himself a propitiation, sanctifying his soul by the mortification of his members.
paragraphs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
paragraphs.work: ON PERFECTION

paragraphs.text: "Whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood, for the showing forth of his righteousness, through the remission of former offenses, in the forbearance of God, for the showing forth of his righteousness at this present time: that he himself may be just, and the one who justifies him who is of the faith of Jesus Christ." When the holy Apostle had taught us many wondrous things about our Lord Jesus Christ, things which are said of him by way of mystery, in this place he has brought forward something still more eminent, which I think is not easily found in other places of Scripture. For whereas above he had said that he gave himself as a redemption for the whole human race, so that he might redeem those who were held in the captivity of sins, since apart from God he tasted death for all, now he adds something more sublime, and says that "God set him forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood": namely, that by the sacrificial offering of his own body he might make God propitious to men, and through this might show forth his righteousness, while he remitted to them their former offenses, which they had contracted by serving the worst of tyrants during that time in which God bore with these things and suffered them to be done.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: But he endured this so that afterward, that is, in this present time, he might show his righteousness. For at the consummation of the age, in the last time, God manifested his righteousness, and gave as redemption him whom he made a propitiator: lest perhaps, if he had sent the propitiator earlier, he might not have reconciled to God so great a number of the human race as in these times in which the world now seems filled with people. For God is just, and being just he could not justify the unjust: therefore he willed that there be the intervention of a propitiator, so that through faith in him those might be justified who could not be justified through their own works.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: Let these things, so far as they pertain to the explanation of the wording itself, be set down first, so that the apostolic reading may become clearer. But now, as is our custom, let us inquire what the inner sense of the apostolic saying contains; and first of all, how it is said: "Whom God set forth as a propitiatory (or propitiator) through faith in his blood." It is certain that in almost every place the Apostle's meaning flows from the treasuries of the Law and the Prophets.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: Let us therefore inquire where he found the term "propitiatory," and from where he took up this name. I recall the Lord speaking to Moses in Exodus and instructing him in what he ought to do: first indeed to command the ark, and that its poles and rings be made along the sides of the ark; and after this he says: "And you shall make a propitiatory of pure gold, two and a half cubits its length, and one and a half cubits its width.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: And you shall make two cherubim of beaten gold, and you shall place them upon each side of the propitiatory: one cherub on this side, and the other cherub on the other side of the propitiatory; and you shall make it so that the two cherubim are on its two sides, spreading out their wings and overshadowing the propitiatory; and their faces shall be toward one another over the propitiatory.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: And you shall make the cherubim, and you shall set the propitiatory upon the ark, and into the ark you shall put the testimonies which I shall give you; and I will make myself known to you from there, and I will speak to you from above the propitiatory, from the midst of the two cherubim which are over the ark of the covenant, according to all that I shall command you for the children of Israel." It plainly appears that the Apostle, having found the name "propitiatory" in these passages, has now placed it in his own Letters, concerning which our discourse is. And it seems that he referred this propitiatory, of which it is written in Exodus, to none other than the Lord Savior, when he says that God set him forth "as a propitiatory through faith." How indeed that which is described in Exodus as made of the purest gold was the form and figure of this true propitiatory is worth investigating.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: And first indeed it must be considered in which places the gold that is used in the work is called pure gold, and in which places gold alone is set down without any addition. Observing this in many places, I seem to myself to have discovered that wherever with the addition it is called pure gold, it indicates that holy and pure soul of Jesus, which "committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth"; and that these measurements of the length and breadth of the propitiatory fit that soul — although it is arduous to explain these things, and to fit to that holy soul each single detail that is reported about the propitiatory.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: First, then, let us see what it says: that the length of the propitiatory had neither two cubits only — a number that is customarily applied to bodies that are joined together and generated — nor three whole cubits, a number that is accustomed to exceed the designation of creature, and to be consecrated to incorporeal nature. Two and a half cubits, then, it calls the length of the propitiatory, and one and a half its breadth.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: Now if in such matters it is lawful to be bold: since the same Apostle says of Christ that he "is the mediator of God and of men," it seems to me that this soul is midway between God and man, being indeed inferior to the nature of the Trinity, having something less, and yet, though it is beneath that, not being mixed with the dual number — which is assigned to those set in a body — apart from the extraordinary and surpassing eminence of its virtues. For this is shown by the fact that its measure is designated as having something above two cubits, though less than three.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: But also as to its breadth being recorded as having one and a half cubits, by this it is indeed described in terms of its monad and singular standing, yet as not having grown wholly into the dual number, which is sometimes even put for things unclean. For although he took up the flesh of our nature, it was nevertheless assumed from an undefiled Virgin, and formed by the chaste operation of the Holy Spirit.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: For this reason, therefore, the Apostle too, when discussing the Mediator, marked a plain distinction, saying: "The mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus"; namely, that he might teach that "mediator" is to be referred not to the deity of Christ, but to the humanity, which is his soul. Its length, therefore, is set down, and its breadth. The length signifies that which reaches toward God and is joined to the Trinity; the breadth, that it dwells among men, who are wont to walk the broad and spacious way; and therefore it is rightly called by the name of Mediator, because, as we have said, this holy soul was midway between the divinity of the Trinity and the frailty of humanity.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: This soul, therefore, can be understood as the propitiatory, according to what we have said above, upon which two cherubim are said to be placed, one on this side and one on the other side. Of what, then, are these two cherubim to be thought to bear the form? For "cherubim," translated into our language, signifies "fullness of knowledge." Where, then, do we speak of a fullness of knowledge, except in him of whom the Apostle says, "In whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge"?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: The Apostle assuredly says these things of the Word of God. But he writes similar things also of the Holy Spirit when he says: "But God has revealed it to us through his Spirit; for the Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God." It is signified, therefore, as I think, in that propitiatory — that is, in the soul of Jesus — that the Word of God, who is the only-begotten Son, and his Holy Spirit dwell there always: and this is what the two cherubim placed upon the propitiatory indicate.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: But observe this also, that he did not say: One cherub on the right side, and the other cherub on the left side; but he says: "One cherub on this side, and the other cherub on the other side" — that he might show that in that propitiatory, that is, in the soul of Christ, there was nothing left-hand. Moreover, these two cherubim are winged; and not only winged, but also spreading out their wings. If any of the saints has deserved to have the highest testimony from God, it is said that God was with him, as is said of Joshua son of Nun: "And God was with him, as he was with Moses his servant." But wherever a promise of a greater gift is given by God, God says: "And I will be in them, and will walk among them." But you will find no soul among men so blessed and so exalted except this one alone, in which the Word of God and the Holy Spirit found so much breadth, so much capacity, that it is said not only to dwell there, but even to spread out its wings, and by a new rite of the mystery at times even to fly.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: Both cherubim are also said to have their faces turned toward one another above this blessed soul, whereby a concordant and harmonious perception of the divinity is poured into it from the Son of God and from the Holy Spirit. But where is this soul set, the soul full of God, in which it pleased all the fullness of the Godhead to dwell? "Above the ark," he says, "of the testament." The ark of the testament can be understood as his holy flesh, in which this blessed soul is placed, having within itself the testimonies of God — by which are understood those sufferings of Christ which he bore in the flesh, foretold long before by the divine testimonies.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: The heavenly powers too can be understood as the ark of God, since they also are indeed capable of receiving the Word of God and the Holy Spirit; yet the soul of Jesus is set above them, and it is through her, in a certain manner, as mediatrix, that they receive the grace of the divine bounty. After this he says: "And I will make myself known to you from thence, and I will speak to you from above the propitiatory." Not to Moses only, but to each one of the saints who is a servant of God, God makes himself known from no other place, nor is he known from any other source, save from that propitiatory which we have expounded above, and from the midst of the cherubim.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: This the prophet Habakkuk also signifies where he says: "In the midst of two living creatures you shall be known; when the years draw near you shall be known, and when the time is at hand you shall be shown forth." For "no one knows the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son shall be pleased to reveal him." But Paul too says that "God has revealed it to us through his Spirit." For this reason, therefore, he says, "I will make myself known to you from thence, and I will speak to you from above the propitiatory, between the two cherubim which are over the ark of the testament." And I think it was not out of place that the things we took from Exodus have been expounded, so that the sense might become plain in what way the Apostle in the present passage has taken up the name "propitiatory," when he says: "Whom God set forth as a propitiatory through faith." But this very word which he used, "set forth" (proposuit), is felt to be said rather of the soul of Jesus than of his deity.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: For "set forth" is understood as though "placed beforehand," that is, before it existed. For what already is, is placed; what does not yet exist is set forth beforehand. It is not fitting, then, that of him who always was — that is, of the Word of God — it should be said that he was set forth; but it is said of his soul, which, although it is inseparable from the Word of God, was nevertheless created, and is posterior to the deity of the Only-begotten. Nor will it seem unfitting that it be said of her that before she existed she was set forth and preordained to be a propitiatory.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: Since, therefore, according to what we have expounded above, "God set forth" Jesus Christ "as a propitiatory through faith in his blood," it seems necessary to inquire from the divine laws what that propitiation is which is made through blood, so that from these things we may be able to gather in what way propitiation has been made through the blood of Jesus also. It is written in Leviticus, after the sacrifice of the high priest: "But if the whole assembly of Israel shall be in ignorance, and the matter be hidden from its eyes, and they shall do one of those things among the Lord's commandments which ought not to be done, and shall offend, and the sin which they have sinned becomes known to them, the assembly shall bring a bull calf from the herd for sin"; and a little later: "And the priest who has been anointed shall bring in of the blood of the calf into the tabernacle of witness"; and again a little later: "And he shall do with the calf," he says, "just as he did with the calf for sin, and the priest shall make propitiation for them, and it shall be forgiven them." Through blood, then, the priest makes propitiation for the whole assembly, that it may be forgiven them. Let us now examine each of the several names which are written concerning the Savior, and let us contemplate more diligently, in each of the titles, what things they are that are designated.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: You will find, therefore, since indeed it pleased all the fullness of the divinity to dwell in him bodily, that he himself is both the propitiatory, and the high priest, and the victim "which is offered for the people." And concerning the propitiatory enough has already been said. But concerning the high priest, David in the Psalm writes plainly, and the apostle Paul to the Hebrews.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: And that he is also the victim, John testifies, saying: "This is the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world." According, therefore, to that whereby he is a victim, propitiation is effected by the pouring out of his blood, in that he gives remission of former offenses; which propitiation, nevertheless, comes to each one of the believers by the way of faith. For unless he were to give remission of former offenses, the propitiation would not be proved to have been effected.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: But since remission of sins is granted, it is certain that the propitiation has been fulfilled by the outpouring of the sacred blood: for "without the shedding of blood," as the Apostle says, "there is no remission" of sins. But lest Paul should seem to you to have been the only one to venture upon the name of propitiation in Christ, hear how John too speaks in harmony with this sense when he says: "My little children, these things I write to you, that you may not sin. But if anyone shall have sinned, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the just; and he is the propitiation for our sins; and not only for ours, but also for those of the whole world." With one and the same sense, therefore, the apostles name Christ "propitiatory," or "propitiation," or — as is more frequently found in the Latin manuscripts — "Propitiator." But it makes no difference whether "propitiator" or "propitiatory" or "propitiation" or even "entreaty" be written, since among the Greeks it is always expressed by one and the same word. Unless perhaps it should seem to some that "propitiation" is his divine substance itself, while "propitiator" is understood of him when he fulfills the dispensations among men. But that also which John said, that "he himself is the entreaty (or propitiation) for our sins; and not only for ours, but also for those of the whole world," seems to have brought us a certain enlargement of the mystery, so as to show that Jesus is the propitiator not only of believers, but of the whole world as well; yet not first of the world, and then ours, but first ours, and only so at last of the whole world.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: For although the whole creation awaits the grace of the Redeemer, nevertheless each one will come to salvation in his own order. This I judge to be indicated in Leviticus also, where the victims of propitiation are commanded to be offered through the high priest. Nor yet in these is a confused order of sacrifices set forth; but first he says what the propitiation is, and what kind of victim is to be offered if the priest has sinned. Second, if the whole assembly has offended through ignorance, with what sort of victims God is appeased. Third, if a ruler has sinned, it is written in what order he is to be purified.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: Fourth, if a single soul has sinned, concerning this too the rite of expiation is set out. These several things, in their mystical understanding, designate by certain fixed orders and modes and causes the future propitiation of Christ, not only for our sins but also for the whole world — provided, however, that one look upon them, illuminated by the Holy Spirit, according to that revelation which is said to have been shown to Moses on the mountain.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: There comes about, therefore, through the propitiation of the blood of Christ, the remission "of former offenses, in the forbearance of God, for the showing forth of his justice." The forbearance of God is where the sinner is not punished the moment he sins, but, according to what the Apostle said in that same place, is led by the patience of God to repentance; and in this God is said to show forth his justice.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: God has set forth Christ in public so that anyone who wants to be redeemed may draw near to him. Christ performs the work of expiation for all who believe that they need to be set free by his blood. Christ died for our former sins in order to reverse God's judgment, by which he had finally determined to punish us for them.
paragraphs.author: Pelagius
paragraphs.work: PELAGIUS'S COMMENTARY ON ROMANS

paragraphs.text:
The mercy seat was gold-plated and placed on top of the ark. On each side was the figure of a cherub. When the high priest approached it, the holy kindness of God was revealed.The apostle teaches us that Christ is the true mercy seat, of which the one in the Old Testament was but a type. The name applies to Christ in his humanity, not in his divinity. For as God Christ responded to the expiation made at the mercy seat. It is as man that he receives this label, just as elsewhere he is called a sheep, a lamb, sin and a curse.
Furthermore, the ancient mercy seat was bloodless because it was inanimate. It could only receive the drops of blood pouring from the sacrificial victims. But the Lord Christ is both God and the mercy seat, both the priest and the lamb, and he performed the work of our salvation by his blood, demanding only faith from us.
paragraphs.author: Theodoret of Cyrus
paragraphs.work: INTERPRETATION OF THE LETTER TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: The present time means our time, in which God has given what long before he had promised to give at the time at which he gave it. Paul has rightly said that God gave what he promised in order to be revealed as righteous. For he had promised that he would justify those who believe in Christ, as he says in Habakkuk: "The righteous will live by faith in me." Whoever has faith in God and Christ is righteous.
paragraphs.author: Ambrosiaster
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON PAUL'S EPISTLES

paragraphs.text: "To declare His righteousness." What is declaring of righteousness? Like the declaring of His riches, not only for Him to be rich Himself, but also to make others rich, or of life, not only that He is Himself living, but also that He makes the dead to live; and of His power, not only that He is Himself powerful, but also that He makes the feeble powerful. So also is the declaring of His righteousness not only that He is Himself righteous, but that He doth also make them that are filled with the putrefying sores of sin suddenly righteous.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on Romans 7

paragraphs.text: And it is to explain this, viz. what is "declaring," that he has added, "That He might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus." Doubt not then: for it is not of works, but of faith: and shun not the righteousness of God, for it is a blessing in two ways; because it is easy, and also open to all men. And be not abashed and shamefaced. For if He Himself openly declareth Himself to do so, and He, so to say, findeth a delight and a pride therein, how comest thou to be dejected and to hide thy face at what thy Master glorieth in?
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on Romans 7

paragraphs.text: And he added well, "at this time"; for in the time of the present age the justice of God lies in forbearance, but in the age to come it lies in retribution. For it seemed just in God's sight that, since he had appointed the age to come for judgment, he should assign the present one to forbearance and patience. For if he punished the sinner in this time, it would not seem just to call again to judgment one whom he had punished. But if he forbears and is patient in the present age, he will rightly be a just judge in the age to come. He justifies, therefore, him who is of faith, just as it is written also concerning Abraham, that "Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him unto justice." But if Abraham believed, and was justified out of faith, it will without doubt follow that now too he who believes God is justified through the faith of Jesus Christ together with faithful Abraham.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: Paul wants to show that God had waited for sinners to reform themselves but that they had abused his patience and gone on to greater sins. The believer in Jesus is the only one who has been found righteous, and God has justified him not by works but by faith.
paragraphs.author: Pelagius
paragraphs.work: PELAGIUS'S COMMENTARY ON ROMANS

paragraphs.text: '" Such and so great futilities of theirs wherewith they flatter God and pander to themselves, effeminating rather than invigorating discipline, with how cogent and contrary (arguments) are we for our part able to rebut,-(arguments) which set before us warningly the "severity" of God, and provoke our own constancy? Because, albeit God is by nature good, still He is "just" too.
paragraphs.author: Tertullian
paragraphs.work: On Modesty

paragraphs.text: Paul tells those who live under the law that they have no reason to boast basing themselves on the law and claiming to be of the race of Abraham, seeing that no one is justified before God except by faith.
paragraphs.author: Ambrosiaster
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON PAUL'S EPISTLES

paragraphs.text: For who will glory, or for what, when everyone has become worthless and gone out of the right way, and nobody does good works anymore? Therefore he says that all glorying is excluded.… How? We have acquired the forgiveness of our former sins and have been justified freely by the mercy and grace of Christ.
paragraphs.author: Cyril of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON ROMANS

paragraphs.text: "Where is boasting then? it is excluded," he says. "By what law? of works? Nay, but by the law of faith." Paul is at great pains to show that faith is mighty to a degree which was never even fancied of the Law. For after he had said that God justifieth man by faith, he grapples with the Law again.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on Romans 7

paragraphs.text: And he does not say, where then are the well doings. of the Jews? where their righteous dealing? but, "where is then the boasting?" so taking every opportunity of showing, that they do but use great words, as though they had somewhat more than others, and have no work to show. And after saying, "Where then is the boasting?" he does not say, it is put out of sight and hath come to an end, but "it is excluded," which word rather expresses unseasonableness; since the reason for it is no more. For as when the judgment is come they that would repent have not any longer the season for it, thus now the sentence being henceforth passed, and all being upon the point of perishing, and He being at hand Who by grace would break these terrors, they had no longer the season for making a plea of amelioration wrought by the Law. See he calls the faith also a law delighting to keep to the names, and so allay the seeming novelty.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on Romans 7

paragraphs.text: But what is the "law of faith?" It is, being saved by grace. Here he shows God's power, in that He has not only saved, but has even justified, and led them to boasting, and this too without needing works, but looking for faith only.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on Romans 7

paragraphs.text: "Where then is your boasting? It has been shut out. By what law? Of works? No, but by the law of faith. For we reckon that a man is justified by faith without the works of the law." Again and yet more often we admonish those who desire to attend more carefully to Paul's writings to hold more tenaciously to that distinction which we spoke of above — how he pursues now the case of circumcision, now that of uncircumcision, that is, of the Jews or of the Gentiles, always along a separate track. For if even a little should escape the reader, at once this narrow and slender footpath of understanding will be thrown into confusion.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: Therefore, when the Apostle had shown above what is the Jew's advantage, or what the usefulness of circumcision, and had taught that to those first ones the oracles of God were entrusted, and by these things had seemed to exalt that vaunting of theirs by which they are wont to raise themselves against the Gentiles; and again, in what follows, had set against these things the objection that the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ is unto all who believe, and that there is no distinction, but that all have sinned, both Jews and Greeks, and lack the glory of God, and are justified through the grace and redemption which is in Christ Jesus; and that he himself is the propitiatory through faith, and that every one who is of faith is justified by him — now at last, setting down as it were the conclusion of his assertions, he says in this place: "Where then is your boasting?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: It has been shut out. By what law? Of works? No, but by the law of faith. For we reckon that a man is justified by faith without the works of the law": and he says that the justification of faith alone suffices, so that one who merely believes is justified, even if no work at all has been completed by him. It presses upon us, therefore, who strive to assert that the Apostle's Scripture is whole and entire, and that all of it stands together in its own order, to inquire who has been justified by faith alone without works.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: So far, then, as concerns an example, I think that thief suffices who, crucified with Christ, cried out to him from the cross: "Lord Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom." Nor is any other good work of his described in the Gospels, but for this faith alone Jesus says to him: "Truly I say to you: Today you shall be with me in paradise." Let us now, if it seems good, fit the words of the apostle Paul to the case of this thief, and say to the Jew: "Where then is your boasting?" Certainly it has been shut out; and shut out not by the law of works, but by the law of faith.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: For by faith this thief was justified without the works of the law: because concerning this the Lord did not inquire what he had previously done; nor did he wait to see what work he might complete once he had believed, but, as he was about to enter paradise, he took him as his companion, justified by confession alone. But also that woman of whom it is related in the Gospel according to Luke, that "when she had learned that Jesus reclined at table in the house of the Pharisee, she brought a vessel of ointment, and standing behind at his feet and weeping, she washed his feet with her tears, and wiped them with the hairs of her head, and kissed them and anointed them with the ointment.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: But the Pharisee who had invited him, seeing this, said within himself: If this man were a prophet, he would surely know who and what sort of woman she is who touches his feet, for she is a sinner." But Jesus spoke to him the parable of the five hundred or the fifty denarii; and from no work of the law, but for faith alone, he says to her: "Your sins are forgiven you"; and again: "Your faith has saved you, go in peace." But also in many places of the Gospel we read that the Savior used this expression, so that he calls the faith of the believer the cause of his salvation.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: From all which it is clear that the Apostle rightly reckons that a man is justified by faith without the works of the law. But perhaps someone hearing these things may grow slack and take up a negligence of doing well, since indeed faith alone suffices for justification. To him we shall say that after justification, if anyone acts unjustly, without doubt he has despised the grace of justification. For no one receives pardon of sins for this purpose, that he should think license to sin has again been given him. For indulgence is granted not for future but for past offenses.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: Therefore, to return to our subject, a man is justified by faith, and the works of the law contribute nothing to him for justification.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: But where there is not the faith which justifies the believer, even if a man has works from the law, yet because they are not built upon the foundation of faith, although they may seem to be good, nevertheless they cannot justify the one who works them, because faith is lacking to them, which is the seal of those who are justified by God, as we said above, because "Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him unto righteousness." So much is this so, that he who is justified by the grace of faith says, according to Paul, that "the grace of God which was given to me was not in vain." Therefore every boasting which comes from the works of the law is shut out. And that what we say may become still more evident, we shall give an example from those things which are written in the Gospel, where the Pharisee and the Publican went up to the temple of God; "and the Pharisee," he says, "standing in the midst, said: God, I give you thanks, because I am not as the rest of men, robbers, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican: I fast twice in the week; I give tithes of all that I possess," and the rest. And these things perhaps he may have said truly, but according to the Lord's sentence, being corrupted by the disease of vaunting, he did not go down from the temple justified.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: Such boasting, therefore, as came from the works of the law is shut out, because it does not have the humility of the cross of Christ; and hear what he says who boasts in that cross: "But far be it from me to boast, save in the cross of my Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world." You see the Apostle not boasting over his righteousness, nor over his chastity, nor over his wisdom, nor over his other virtues or acts, but most openly declaring and saying: "He who boasts, let him boast in the Lord." And thus Jewish boasting has been shut out, not by the law of works, but by the law of faith which is in Christ Jesus, in whose cross the Apostle boasts.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: For who will rightly boast even over his own chastity, when he reads it written, that "if anyone looks upon a woman to desire her, he has already committed adultery with her in his heart"? Whence also the prophet says: "How shall anyone boast that he has a chaste heart?" Or who will boast over wisdom, when he sees it written, that "the world through wisdom did not know God: and therefore it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe"?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: And again: "The foolish things of the world God has chosen, that he may confound the wise"? And who will boast even over his own righteousness, when he hears God saying through the prophet, that "all your righteousness is as the cloth of a menstruous woman"?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: The only just boasting, therefore, is in the faith of the cross of Christ, which shuts out all that boasting which comes down from the works of the law. And these things have been said by us because the Apostle spoke as it were in the language of one questioning: "Where then is your boasting?" And to this he himself answered himself: "It has been shut out." And again, as though he were questioning himself, he says: "By what law? Of works?" And he answered himself: "No, but by the law of faith. For we reckon that a man is justified by faith without the works of the law." Of these things we have already spoken above.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: But as to the fact that in the present place also he makes mention again of two laws, and speaks of the law of works and the law of faith, consider also for yourself, you who read, whether this discourse ought to be inclined toward the law of Moses and the natural law, or toward the law of the letter and the law of the spirit: because the law of the letter kills, and works death; but the law of the spirit of life sets free from the law of sin and death.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: Now you say to me (says Paul), What new law has thrown the old one out? For when the ruler adds to the law, the law is changed. Paul answers: When the law of works came in it did not abolish the former law—on the contrary, it actually contained the former law. But when the law of faith appeared it did abolish the earlier law, having overcome the boasting which came from the law of works. These things have been given to us by the grace of God, which our forefathers, however hard they may have tried, were unable to obtain.
paragraphs.author: Theodore of Mopsuestia
paragraphs.work: PAULINE COMMENTARY FROM THE GREEK CHURCH

paragraphs.text: By "boasting" Paul means the proud spirits of the Jews and their excessive arrogance. For they thought they were the only ones who enjoyed God's providence. But after the divine grace appeared and spread to all nations, the boasting of the Jews ceased.… Paul calls faith a law, recalling the words of the prophet Jeremiah: "Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the House of Israel and the House of Judah, not like the covenant which I made with their fathers."
paragraphs.author: Theodoret of Cyrus
paragraphs.work: INTERPRETATION OF THE LETTER TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: Paul says that a Gentile can be sure that he is justified by faith without doing the works of the law, e. g., circumcision or new moons or the veneration of the sabbath.
paragraphs.author: Ambrosiaster
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON PAUL'S EPISTLES

paragraphs.text: This must not be understood in such a way as to say that a man who has received faith and continues to live is righteous, even though he leads a wicked life.
paragraphs.author: Augustine of Hippo
paragraphs.work: QUESTIONS 76.1

paragraphs.text: "Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the Law." When he had shown that by faith they were superior to the Jews, then he goes on with great confidence to discourse upon it also, and what seemed therein to annoy he again heals up. For these two things were what confused the Jews; one, if it were possible for men, who with works were not saved, to be saved without them, and another, if it were just for the uncircumcised to enjoy the same blessings with those, who had during so long a period been nurtured in the Law; which last confused them more by far than the former.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on Romans 7

paragraphs.text: And on this ground having proved the former, he goes on to the other next, which perplexed the Jews so far, that they even complained on account of this position against Peter after they believed. What does he say then? "Therefore we conclude, that by faith a man is justified." He does not say, a Jew, or one under the Law, but after leading forth his discourse into a large room, and opening the doors of faith to the world, he says "a man," the name common to our race.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on Romans 7

paragraphs.text: Some people misinterpret this verse in order to do away with the works of righteousness, saying that faith by itself is enough, even though Paul says elsewhere: "If I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing." If this seems to contradict the sense of the other [verses], what works did the apostle mean when he said that a man is justified by faith, without works? Obviously, these are the works of circumcision, the sabbath and so on, and not the works of righteousness about which St. James says: "Faith without works is dead." [In this verse] Paul is speaking about the man who comes to Christ and is saved when he first believes by faith alone. But by adding the works of the law Paul is saying that there are also works of grace which believers ought to perform.
paragraphs.author: Pelagius
paragraphs.work: PELAGIUS'S COMMENTARY ON ROMANS

paragraphs.text: Paul did not say "we hold" because he was himself uncertain. He said it in order to counter those who concluded from this that anyone who wished to could be justified simply by willing faith. Note carefully that Paul does not say simply "without the law," as if we could just perform virtue by wanting to, nor do we do the works of the law by force. We do them because we have been led to do them by Christ.
paragraphs.author: Theodore of Mopsuestia
paragraphs.work: PAULINE COMMENTARY FROM THE GREEK CHURCH

paragraphs.text: Undoubtedly there is only one God for everybody. For even the Jews cannot claim that their God is not the God of the Gentiles also, because they believe that the origin of all people is from the one Adam and that no one who comes willingly to the law may be prevented from accepting it. Some Gentiles actually went with the Israelites into the desert of Egypt, and the Israelites were ordered to accept them as long as they agreed to be circumcised and eat unleavened bread, or the Passover, together with the rest of them. Then again Cornelius, a Gentile who was not judaized, received the gift of God, and it is clear from holy Scripture that he was justified.
paragraphs.author: Ambrosiaster
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON PAUL'S EPISTLES

paragraphs.text: Wherefore also, to those that ask the wisdom that is with us, we are to hold out things suitable, that with the greatest possible ease they may, through their own ideas, be likely to arrive at faith in the truth. For "I became all things to all men, that I might gain all men." Since also "the rain" of the divine grace is sent down "on the just and the unjust." "Is He the God of the Jews only, and not also of the Gentiles? Yes, also of the Gentiles: if indeed He is one God," exclaims the noble apostle.
paragraphs.author: Clement of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: The Stromata Book 5

paragraphs.text: One righteous man, then, differs not, as righteous, from another righteous man, whether he be of the Law or a Greek. For God is not only Lord of the Jews, but of all men, and more nearly the Father of those who know Him. For if to live well and according to the law is to live, also to live rationally according to the law is to live; and those who lived rightly before the Law were classed under faith, and judged to be righteous,-it is evident that those, too, who were outside of the Law, having lived rightly, in consequence of the peculiar nature of the voice, though they are in Hades and in ward, on hearing the voice of the Lord, whether that of His own person or that acting through His apostles, with all speed turned and believed. For we remember that the Lord is "the power of God," and power can never be weak.
paragraphs.author: Clement of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: The Stromata Book 6

paragraphs.text: "Is He the God of the Jews only?" As if he said, On what foot does it then seem to you amiss that every man should be saved? Is God partial? So showing from this, that in wishing to flout the Gentiles, they are rather offering an insult to God's glory, if, that is, they would not allow Him to be the God of all. But if He is of all, then He taketh care of all; and if He care for all, then He saveth all alike by faith. And this is why he says, "Is He the God of the Jews only? is He not also of the Gentiles? Yes, of the Gentiles also." For He is not partial as the fables of the Gentiles (cf. Ov. Tr. I. ii. 5. sqq) are, but common to all, and One...
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on Romans 7

paragraphs.text: Hence he also fittingly adds in what follows: "Or is he the God of the Jews only? Is he not also of the Gentiles?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: Yes, of the Gentiles also. Since indeed there is one God, who justifies the circumcision from faith, and the uncircumcision through faith." For those who would have the God of the Jews to be one and the God of the Gentiles another — that is, one God of the Law and another of the Gospels — the reply on this point will be narrow and confining enough, since the apostle Paul gives his verdict abundantly enough when he not only says that there is one God of Jews and of Gentiles, but also adds that it is one and the same God who justifies the circumcision from faith and the uncircumcision through faith.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: And if they should wish to take "circumcision" by way of allegory, so as to say that by this word he called all the holy and spiritual ones, they will at once find a stumbling block in what follows. For if he called the holy ones — or, as they name them, the spiritual ones — "circumcision," it follows that by "uncircumcision" he meant sinners, whom they call "animal" (of the soul). And how will it be fitting that the good God should justify spiritual and animal alike? For them, then, there will be an inextricable knot in these words of the Apostle.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: But according to us, who say that "circumcision" means those who have believed from among the Jews, and "uncircumcision" no less means those who have been called from among the Gentiles to the faith, the exposition will be plain and easy. For it is one and the same God who justifies believers from either people, not by the privilege of circumcision or of uncircumcision, but by the regard for faith alone. There remains also the difference of a single syllable, in which the Apostle seems to have varied his expression. Let it not pass us by idly that he says God justifies the circumcision from faith, and not through faith; but the uncircumcision through faith, and not from faith.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: For this exchange of prepositions does not seem to me to be held superfluous in his usage, since we find that in other places too they are set down by him not at random but observantly, and that the difference of this distinction is of necessity preserved — as when, speaking of God, he says: "Since from him, and through himself, and in him are all things." And again elsewhere he says: "For as the woman is from the man, so also the man is through the woman; but all things are from God." Of the same sort is what he writes to the Corinthians: "To one indeed through the Spirit is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit." And not only does the apostle Paul maintain the observance of these distinctions, but John also, who, though he says of the Word of God that "all things were made through him," testifies that life was made not through him but in him, saying: "That which was made, in him was life." And since it would take much to expound the passages we have now brought forward by way of example, let us gather their sense briefly, so far as our capacity allows.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: When it is said "from him," something primary seems to be shown by the beginning of this preposition.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
paragraphs.work: COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

paragraphs.text: But when "through him" is said, the understanding of a subsequent cause is designated — that is, of the cause which comes after the primary one.
